findings.title: Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The cleanup loop ticker is changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, so every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, query history, etc.) runs ten times as often. `clean` is synchronous and can take up to the 9-minute timeout; because ticker events are buffered as one pending tick, a long-running cleanup can be followed immediately by another, effectively running cleanup continuously and increasing database load/contention. Unless a tenfold increase in global cleanup frequency is intended and coordinated, this change should be reverted.

findings.title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at error level with full ID lists
findings.body: The new batch code logs normal, successful cleanup work with `r.log.Error` and includes the entire `ids` slice and generated `cond`. This occurs in `CleanAnnotations` (by age and count) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). On a table with many matching rows a single log line can contain tens of thousands of IDs, every cleanup cycle, even when `err` is nil. This floods error logs/alerting and can slow the cleanup job itself. Use Debug/Trace and log counts or errors, not full ID lists.

findings.title: New SQLite batch-size test does not actually exceed SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER
findings.body: The new test case creates 40,003 annotations, but cleanup is run per annotation type and each type has only about 13,334 rows. Therefore no DELETE statement ever contains more than about 13,334 IDs, which is below SQLite >=3.32's 32,766 parameter limit. The test would still pass if the large-batch/inlining fallback were removed, so it does not verify the boundary it claims to cover. It needs more than 32,766 annotations of a single type (or an equivalent setup producing a single batch above the limit).

findings.title: SQLite large-batch ID list is built in quadratic time
findings.body: In the SQLite fallback, the ID list is materialized with repeated `fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`, which copies the entire growing string on every iteration. This makes construction O(n^2) in the number of IDs; a batch in the tens of thousands can copy gigabytes and create GC pressure during cleanup. Use `strings.Builder`, a byte slice, or `strings.Join` to build the list in linear time.
